Topics include: basics of photography as applied to manual filmmaking, exposure to contemporary filmmakers, generating images (moving and still) within conceptual frameworks which respond to contemporary issues. Super 8mm Cameras will be checked out to you. Repeatable to a maximum of 12 credits, including original course.
ART 378: A broad introduction to the various roles an art educator plays in the artistic lives of young people. For those interested in teaching art, in or out of schools, this course will develop knowledge and understanding of artistic development in childhood and adolescence (K-12), curriculum design and assessment, diversity, equity, accessibility, and inclusion in art education spaces, art education advocacy, and the intersection of material & process exploration, visual & cultural literacy, and personal meaning-making in diverse art education contexts.
ART 381: Identity work becomes central to art-making for middle and high school students, and in this course, students will develop a deeper understanding of adolescent development within the context of the art classroom, including theories of adolescent artistic development and the alignment of curricula, lesson planning, and evaluation/assessment accordingly. Students will also explore their own identity as teachers and build a personal, self-reflective practice toward resilience prior to entering the classroom.
ART 384: This course explores a series of issues central to the work of teaching with art, including the layered interpretations of art objects, balancing viewer responses and “official” information, fostering visual literacy among students and museum visitors, culturally-responsive teaching with works of art, and the inclusion of non-discursive activities in museum teaching.
ART 385: This course introduces major theories, artworks, tools, and techniques that are commonly associated with digital, time-based interdisciplinary art practices.
ART 386: This hands-on digital video production class is designed for a range of skill levels, from beginners to more advanced video makers. During this project-based class, students will be exposed to a broad range of experimental video works, and will learn and develop production and post-production skills.
ART 387: This studio class will explore experimental techniques associated with 2D animation. During this project-based class, students will be exposed to a broad range of animation styles including, but not limited to: hand/digitally drawn, stop-motion, pixilation, collage (cut-out), and rotoscoping. The tools and final project output will utilize the digital format. Repeatable to a maximum of 15 credits, including original course.
ART 394: This study abroad course is led by a faculty member to provide students with international, experiential learning. An immersive course that takes place in Central and Northern Italy. In this class we explore Italian art and culture focusing on the arts and architecture in Florence, Tuscany, and Venice. Students engage in visual exploration and creative problem solving through a variety of media, tools, and techniques. The class emphasizes drawing, photography, time based art, mixed media, and other portable methods of art making while traveling. Students will participate in both classroom and applied learning opportunities that may include: pre-travel orientation and class meetings at Western, group instruction, reading, writing, and critical reflection assignments, learning from the host community, cultural excursions, field work, post-travel debriefing, and culminating projects.
ART 396: Study traditional and contemporary culture in Japan. Activities include: visiting historical sites, galleries, museums and artist studios. Experience a tea ceremony, papermaking, weaving, natural dyeing and more. Students will contribute to an exhibition following the trip. Offered summer quarter only.
ART 397V: Sound & Motion is a three­week intensive designed to immerse art/non­art students into inter­media production, including sound, film, video, performance. The course will incorporate and recontextualize pop & sub­culture media into contemporary artmaking practices, as well as re­engaging historical toolsets. Elevating contemporary culture production methods (social media, ubiquitous image and sound recording, mash­up appropriation, digital cinema), by re­animating their historical origins (field recording, chance operations, Fluxus, Super 8 & 16mm filmmaking), students will create soundworks, moving picture works, digital inter­media works, and performative action works. The intensive will culminate in a digital archive portfolio/catalogue, and companion zine.
ART 398: This arts education course provides future teachers with a foundation in the elements and principles of Visual Art, Dance, Music and Theatre and their applicability to the elementary classroom. (Also offered as DNC 398, MUS 398 and THTR 398).
ART 400: An individualized course of study not available through or replacing existing curriculum, to be arranged between one matriculating student and sponsoring faculty member. All academic policies and registration deadlines apply. Directed Independent Study courses cannot substitute for General University Requirements and are not eligible for tuition waiver.
ART 422: Development of individual projects in painting and/or drawing through independent studio practice. Studio work is complemented by: discussion of pertinent topics in historical and contemporary painting and drawing, critiques, readings, field trips and guest lectures. Repeatable to a maximum of 10 credits.
ART 431: Self-directed, project-oriented advanced work. Working closely with instructor, students will concentrate on the development of their discipline and artistic production as a personal mode of creative research, in the general context of contemporary art practices. Lecture/lab. Repeatable to a maximum of 15 credits.
ART 437: This study abroad course is led by a faculty member to provide students with international, experiential learning. Students will participate in both classroom and applied learning opportunities that may include: pre-travel orientation and class meetings at Western, group instruction, reading, writing, and critical reflection assignments, learning from the host community, cultural excursions, field work, post-travel debriefing, and culminating projects.
ART 441: Problems in advanced ceramics; self-directed projects and weekly seminars. Repeatable to a maximum of 15 cr.
ART 460: Advanced problems in fiber/fabrics study. Emphasis on self-directed project development and contemporary issues in fibers/fabrics. Repeatable to a maximum of 15 cr.
ART 470: Using a small group dynamic to critique and exchange ideas based on readings, visiting artists and theoretical inquiry, this class explores contemporary concepts surrounding the production of photography. The course consists of self-directed projects, which afford students time to produce a substantial body of research-driven work which reflects their individual interests. Repeatable to a maximum of 15 credits, including original course.
ART 482: Explorations in art media and their adaptation to use in the school. Not to be used for graduate program. Repeatable to a maximum of 15 cr.
ART 492: BFA students will develop a self-directed body of work under the supervision of their faculty committee, independently researching the materials, techniques, processes, subject matter, critical issues and related artistic production that will contribute to their creative project. Students will be required to exhibit their works at the end of the BFA Year. They will prepare their work for presentation and will research materials, display methods, installation formats and venues. Repeatable to a maximum of 9 credits, including original course.
ART 494: Critique-driven, production-oriented interdisciplinary course based in self-directed project development with an emphasis on contemporary issues in studio art. Repeatable to a maximum of 15 credits. This course has been approved for study abroad.
ART 495: For the student who anticipates graduation and completion of the Studio Art BA degree in the near future. Designed to facilitate entry into the world of professional artists, galleries, critics, and curators, with an emphasis on survival skills for the emerging artist. Includes current trends, professional issues and practices, and the preparation of a complete portfolio.
ART 497A: sr or BFA status + 15 cr 300-lvl studio crses
ART 498: ART 498 is an advanced studio seminar for the BFA student that addresses issues in studio practice and facilitates the development of an individual body of work. Repeatable to a maximum of 15 credits, including original course.
ASLC 100: This course provides practice in ASL conversational skills, regarding learning and giving signs as well as receiving signs and basic signs for everyday living, specifically in North America. This course focuses on culture, historical aspects of deafness and the development of a variety of supports for the deaf community, in the United States.
ASLC 101: This course provides practice in ASL conversational skills, regarding learning and giving signs as well as receiving signs and basic signs for everyday living. In addition, this course focuses upon worldwide deaf culture, historical aspects of deafness and the development of a variety of supports for the deaf community, especially in developing countries. ASL is the primary sign language used in West Africa and Southeast Asia. The course also provides for exploration of other systems of sign communication used internationally.
ASLC 102: This beginning sign language course is a continuation of Elementary ASL/Culture. It provides continuing information and practice in conversational skills. In addition, the course continues the exploration of deaf culture, specifically in the US.
ASLC 103: This beginning sign language course is a continuation of Elementary ASL II. It provides continuing information and practice in ASL conversational skills. In addition, the course continues the exploration of deaf culture in the US.
ASTR 103: A survey of astronomy including stars, galactic structure and cosmology. Not recommended for science, math or computer science majors.
ASTR 113: Introduction to the Solar System. Topics include the motion of objects in the sky, seasons, phases of the Moon and eclipses, and the properties of the Sun, planets, and moons with discussion of recent results from space missions. Some class sessions will be held in the planetarium. Open to all students.
ASTR 300: An individualized course of study not available through or replacing existing curriculum, to be arranged between one matriculating student and sponsoring faculty member. All academic policies and registration deadlines apply. Directed Independent Study courses cannot substitute for General University Requirements and are not eligible for tuition waiver.
ASTR 315: Introduction to the modern physical understanding of the Solar System. Topics include gravity, orbits, the formation of stars and planets, planetary atmospheres and surfaces, physical processes in the Solar System.
ASTR 316: Observational evidence of the nature of stars; star formation and star death; structure and kinematics of the Milky Way and other galaxies.
ASTR 320: Large-scale structure of the universe; black holes and active galaxies; curved spacetime; evolution of the expanding universe; the Big Bang and the early universe.
ASTR 397: Operation of manual and computerized telescope systems, including the WWU 12-inch Meade LX 200. Astronomical units and coordinate systems. Basic optics and detector theory. Planning planetarium shows and observations or public outreach. Course meeting schedule will depend on weather.
ASTR 400: An individualized course of study not available through or replacing existing curriculum, to be arranged between one matriculating student and sponsoring faculty member. All academic policies and registration deadlines apply. Directed Independent Study courses cannot substitute for General University Requirements and are not eligible for tuition waiver.
ASTR 416: Application of physics to stars, nebulae and galaxies. Radiation; atomic spectra and chemical abundances in stellar atmospheres and gaseous nebulae; nuclear synthesis in stars; stellar evolution.
BIOL 101: Major ideas and processes of modern biological science at molecular, cellular, organismal and community levels; stressing qualitative and quantitative dimensions of the discipline in lecture, laboratory, field and discussion settings. Lab included. Intended for non-science majors. This course has been approved for study abroad.
BIOL 194: An examination of environmental and biological factors that affect the distribution, abundance, and diversity of marine organisms, using local marine habitats to examine ecological patterns. Open to College Quest students.
BIOL 195: A field-based introduction to marine biology for entering first-year students. S/U grading.
BIOL 204: Introduction to evolutionary and ecological processes involved in the generation of our planet's biodiversity, including review of patterns and processes that influence the origin, evolution, distribution, and abundance of living things. Lab included.
BIOL 205: Structure and function of biomolecules and cells, membrane structure and function, photosynthesis and respiration, molecular origin of life, phylogenetic and metabolic diversity of prokaryotes, molecular genetics and genomics. Lab included.
BIOL 206: Study of the many ways that eukaryotic organisms perform basic functions and cope with varying environmental conditions. Phylogenetic organismal diversity and organ system structural and functional diversity will be studied in lecture and laboratory. Lab included.
BIOL 245: General microbiology with an emphasis on health related issues. Students will learn aseptic technique in lab and the characteristics of microbes that affect human health. Credits earned in this course cannot be applied towards a Biology degree. Lab included.
BIOL 297A: General microbiology with an emphasis on health related issues. Students will learn asceptic technique in lab and the characteristics of microbes that affect human health.
BIOL 300: An individualized course of study not available through or replacing existing curriculum, to be arranged between one matriculating student and sponsoring faculty member. All academic policies and registration deadlines apply. Directed Independent Study courses cannot substitute for General University Requirements and are not eligible for tuition waiver.
BIOL 321: Survey of classical genetics, molecular genetics and genomics.
BIOL 322: Uses prokaryotic and eukaryotic model organisms to explore the fundamentals of genetics and the use of genetics as a tool for basic research. Includes lecture. Lab included.
BIOL 323: Cell structure and function. Topics include: protein structure and function, gene regulation, cell cycle, signal transduction, and organelle assembly and function.
BIOL 324: An introduction to widely used molecular biology techniques and laboratory skills. Lab included.
BIOL 325: Interactions between organisms and their environment, focusing on fundamental concepts in physiological, population, community, and ecosystem ecology.
BIOL 326: Introduction to ecological research, culminating in student-designed research projects. Written and oral presentation of projects. Lab included.
BIOL 327: This course covers the molecular flow of genetic information, including transcription, translation, DNA replication and repair, chromatin structure, and regulation of gene expression.
BIOL 328: This course covers eukaryotic cell structure and function; topics include protein sorting in organelles, cellular organization, cell signaling, growth regulation and mass and energy exchange across biomembranes.
BIOL 340: The design of biological experiments and appropriate statistical analysis of experimental data.
BIOL 345: Cell structure, metabolism, evolution and ecology of prokaryotes.
BIOL 346: Techniques of general microbiology, including isolation, culture, enumeration and identification of prokaryotes. Includes lecture. Lab included.
BIOL 348: Macroscopic and histological examination of human anatomical systems, and study of general neuromuscular and cardiopulmonary functions. Includes lab. Credits earned in this course cannot be applied towards a BA or BS in Biology, except for: Biology - Biomedical Sciences I Concentration, Biology - Biomedical Sciences II Concentration, Biology - Secondary Education Concentration, Biology/Anthropology, BS, and Anthropology/Biology, BA.
BIOL 349: A comprehensive introduction to the study of integrated functions of cells, organs and organ systems in humans. Lab included.
BIOL 397A: Students will be introduced to the basic tenets of tropical marine biology, Mexican culture and traditions, and how to work with other students in close quarters and a new environment.
BIOL 400: An individualized course of study not available through or replacing existing curriculum, to be arranged between one matriculating student and sponsoring faculty member. All academic policies and registration deadlines apply. Directed Independent Study courses cannot substitute for General University Requirements and are not eligible for tuition waiver.
BIOL 401: This course will explore some molecular mechanisms underlying the disease pathology of neurodegeneration, to give insight into how age, genes and risk factors may contribute to common cellular pathologies and diverse disease presentations.
BIOL 403: Physiological and biochemical adaptations of animals to environmental factors. Marine environments are emphasized, but adaptations to fresh water and terrestrial conditions also are considered. Laboratories introduce research techniques which are then applied in student-designed independent research projects. Lab included.
BIOL 404: This course will explore the intrinsic connections between changes in development and the evolution of complex organisms. We will examine how aspects of development can promote or constrain evolutionary potential and explore why multicellular species are composed of groups of traits that develop and evolve together. We will also study the development of Evo-Devo as a field of study.
BIOL 405: Study of microbial communities in aquatic and terrestrial environments, with emphasis on the functional role of microbes in energy flow, nutrient cycling and element transformation. Overview of microbial interactions with eukaryotic hosts. Discussion of structure, genetics, and community on microbial communities. Offered in alternate years.
BIOL 406: Biological oceanography is the study of how organisms affect and are affected by the physics, chemistry, and geology of the oceanographic system. This course will provide a process-oriented view of marine pelagic ecosystems. Oceanographic processes covered in this course will include ocean circulation, biogeography, energetics, food webs, biogeochemical cycles, benthic-pelagic coupling, and plankton ecology.
BIOL 407: The structure and function of marine ecosystems with an emphasis on processes in shallow-water and benthic habitats. Investigative field and laboratory studies of local marine and estuarine systems. Lab included.
BIOL 408: Students will learn instrumentation and methodology for field research, and practice it in a field setting. Lab included.
BIOL 410: Investigation of the component processes and adaptive functions of animal behavior in an ecological and evolutionary context, and an introduction to the questions asked, hypotheses proposed and methods used in the study of animal behavior. Offered in alternate years.
BIOL 412: An investigation into the biology underlying different modes of animal communication, including visual, acoustic, chemical, and tactile signaling behavior. The course will focus on the evolutionary and ecological significance of animal signals and discuss how communication is controlled by different mechanisms (using insights from endocrinology, genetics, and neuroscience) and how these behaviors are impacted by anthropogenic interactions.
BIOL 416: Investigation of the factors controlling whole ecosystem processes such as productivity, decomposition, and nutrient cycling. Application of these concepts to current issues in global change, including the carbon cycle and global warming, land use change, nitrogen-loading, and biodiversity and ecosystem function. Lectures and textbook reading are integrated with discussion of papers from the primary literature.
BIOL 425: Students will explore basic concepts in population and quantitative genetics, and focus on approaches to dissecting genetic variation in ecologically important traits across multiple scales. These concepts and approaches are broadly applicable to many areas of biology; thus readings range in topic from microbes to plants and animals.
BIOL 432: Principles, patterns, processes and mechanisms of evolution.
BIOL 437: This study abroad course is led by a faculty member to provide students with international, experiential learning. Students will participate in both classroom and applied learning opportunities that may include: pre-travel orientation and class meetings at Western, group instruction, reading, writing, and critical reflection assignments, learning from the host community, cultural excursions, field work, post-travel debriefing, and culminating projects.
BIOL 444: The Biology Department Seminar Series provides opportunities for undergraduate students to learn about the latest developments in key fields of biological research. Students will be required to attend seminars and provide a written synopsis of each presentation. Not repeatable for credit.
BIOL 445: This literature-based course will cover the role of bacteria and fungi in symbioses ranging from mutualistic to pathogenic with eukaryotic hosts (including humans and their microbiomes). We will discuss the ecology, evolution, biochemistry, and cellular biology of symbiotic interactions. We will focus on the most current experimental approaches for investigating host-microbe interactions at the molecular and cellular level.
BIOL 446: Cellular and molecular components of innate and adaptive immune responses, cellular and humoral immunity, and discussion of immunological diseases and therapies.
BIOL 447: This small lecture course explores our current understanding of the molecular and cellular mechanisms of cancer development, as well as current therapies used to treat cancer.
BIOL 451: An examination of the molecular basis of plant development and the applied uses of recent discoveries on crop improvement strategies. Emphasis on discussion of primary literature. Offered alternate years.
BIOL 452: Taxonomy of higher plants with emphasis on the characteristics and phylogeny of flowering plant families; collection and identification of local species. Lab included.
BIOL 453: This course examines the biology of the true fungi, including systematics, life history traits, ecology, physiology, and evolutionary biology. The course includes field components. Lab included.
BIOL 456: Physiology and ecology of macroalgae and phytoplankton including identification, collection and culture of major algal groups. Laboratory focuses on research techniques which are then applied in student independent projects. Lab included.
BIOL 460: Evolutionary relationships of invertebrate animals, including anatomy, physiology, classification, development and ecology. Lab included.
BIOL 462: The biology of insects, emphasizing their ecology and evolution, as well as comparative anatomy, physiology, and development. Laboratory exercises will focus on community studies and insect identification. Lab included.
BIOL 464: Examination of the evolution, physiology, ecology and conservation of marine mammals through critical thinking and discussion of the primary literature. Offered in alternate years.
BIOL 470: Examines the development and application of genome-based experimental approaches in biology.
BIOL 473: A seminar course examining the structure, replication and expression of genetic information that focuses on recent advances in gene expression.
BIOL 475: This seminar course explores scientific research on the cellular and molecular mechanisms by which naturally occurring variation in genes results in medically, agriculturally, and evolutionarily important trait variation.
BIOL 476: Examination of the structure of membrane transport proteins and their role in physiological processes through presentation and critical discussion of primary literature. Offered in alternate years.
BIOL 477: Introduction to the design and analysis of genomic research experiments. Genomics is the application of high-throughput molecular biology and bioinformatic techniques to questions in biology. Focus topics include genome assembly, differential gene expression, and genome-wide association studies. Primarily a computer lab course aimed at developing practical bioinformatics skills. Lab included.
BIOL 480: An in-depth introduction to the analysis of sequence data at the gene level that combines concepts and theory in bioinformatics, molecular biology, and molecular evolution with applied skills development via computer-based exercises. Lab included.
BIOL 482: An examination of the molecular, cellular and genetic aspects of developmental biology in invertebrate and vertebrate model systems: fruit flies, nematodes, sea urchins, frogs and mammals.
BIOL 484: Laboratory investigations of cellular and developmental processes. Tissue culture methods and microscopy techniques, including immunofluorescence. Lectures will focus on optics and image processing. Lab included.
BIOL 486: Molecular analysis of developmental processes controlling the formation of functional neural circuits. Emphasis placed on critical evaluation and discussion of primary literature.
BIOL 487: Course-based research experience in which students will undertake novel lab projects investigating the molecular basis of cell biology using molecular biological and biochemical methods, such as PCR genotyping and Western blotting. Discussions will focus on data analysis, model building, and technical background.
BIOL 490: Students will strengthen their understanding of human anatomy and physiology (A/P) by assisting the instructor(s) as a Teaching Intern in BIOL 348 Human Anatomy and Physiology laboratories. Serving as a Teaching Intern also represents a third academic quarter in which students are actively applying their knowledge in Human A/P, which will satisfy the requirement by some graduate programs for a full year of Human A/P. Repeatability to a maximum of 4 credits, including original course.
BIOL 495: Analysis and written and/or oral presentation of results of individual scientific research. Communication can be in the form of a full scientific paper, a poster, or an oral presentation. Number of credits is dependent on the form of communication. Repeatable to a maximum of 6 credits including original course.
BIOL 496: Full- or part-time work with a cooperating agency or firm. Written reports required. Repeatable to a maximum of 8 cr. S/U grading.
BIOL 497Z: This is a literature- and discussion-based course that examines the unifying principles of calcium signaling in biological systems. Topics include the mechanisms of calcium intracellular homeostasis, calcium signal coding/decoding in biological systems, and calcium’s signaling role in physiological and pathological processes.
BIOL 498: Classroom experience in biology teaching. Students will assist faculty in the laboratory and lecture settings. Repeatable to a maximum of 4 cr. S/U grading.
BIOL 500: An individualized course of study not available through or replacing existing curriculum, to be arranged between one matriculating student and sponsoring faculty member. All academic policies and registration deadlines apply.
BIOL 501: This course will explore some molecular mechanisms underlying the disease pathology of neurodegeneration, to give insight into how age, genes and risk factors may contribute to common cellular pathologies and diverse disease presentations.
BIOL 502: This course provides graduate students with a structured yet flexible opportunity to engage in research activities tailored to their individual research interests. The course supports students in developing research techniques, analytical approaches, and conceptual understanding within their biological subfields. Repeatable to a maximum of 16 credits and 4 times, including original course.
BIOL 504: This course will explore the intrinsic connections between changes in development and the evolution of complex organisms. We will examine how aspects of development can promote or constrain evolutionary potential and explore why multicellular species are composed of groups of traits that develop and evolve together. We will also study the development of Evo-Devo as a field of study.
BIOL 506: Biological oceanography is the study of how organisms affect and are affected by the physics, chemistry, and geology of the oceanographic system. This course will provide a process-oriented view of marine pelagic ecosystems. Oceanographic processes covered in this course will include ocean circulation, biogeography, energetics, food webs, biogeochemical cycles, benthic-pelagic coupling, and plankton ecology.
BIOL 508: Analysis and discussion of current literature on selected topics in marine and estuarine biology. Examples of topics include symbiosis, intertidal community dynamics and marine microbiology. Repeatable with different topics.
BIOL 509: Study of microbial communities in aquatic, terrestrial and extreme environments, with emphasis on the functional role of microbes in terms of energy flow, nutrient cycling and biogeochemical transformations. Discussions of community structure and diversity, evolutionary history, and phylogenetic relationships will be covered. All students will be asked to put together a literature review on a topic of interest within the broad umbrella of microbial ecology.
BIOL 512: An investigation into the biology underlying different modes of animal communication, including visual, acoustic, chemical, and tactile signaling behavior. The course will focus on the evolutionary and ecological significance of animal signals and discuss how communication is controlled by different mechanisms (using insights from endocrinology, genetics, and neuroscience) and how these behaviors are impacted by anthropogenic interactions.
BIOL 513: Physiological and biochemical adaptations of animals to environmental factors. Emphasizes marine environments, but adaptations to freshwater and terrestrial environments conditions are also considered. Labs introduce research techniques which are applied in student-designed independent research projects.
BIOL 516: Investigates the factors controlling whole ecosystem processes. Application of these concepts to current issues in global change, including the carbon cycle and global warming, land-use change, nitrogen load, and biodiversity and ecosystem functioning.
BIOL 520: Part of the core curriculum for all Biology MS students. This course is an overview of departmental resources and guidelines for navigating the Biology MS in a timely fashion, with workshops for developing skills in research and teaching (including developing an inclusive learning environment in the classroom) in the biological sciences.
BIOL 521: Part of the core curriculum for all Biology MS students. First-year graduate students will learn the basics of development of a research proposal. This course will focus on evaluating the background literature necessary to develop a thesis proposal and developing and clearly articulating research questions.
BIOL 522: Part of the core curriculum for all Biology MS students. This course is an introduction to developing and writing research proposals and obtaining funding in the Biological Sciences.
BIOL 523: Part of the core curriculum for all Biology MS students. This course helps students develop critical thinking skills related to their thesis research and biology research in general. Repeatable to a maximum of 4 credits, including original course.
BIOL 524: This class provides a practical introduction to how genetic methods can be used to address problems in ecology and evolution. As an applied course this class will stress general concepts of population genetics, phylogenetics, and comparative genomics via the use of qualitative tools in practical exercises while putting less emphasis on the theoretical details underlying these tools.
BIOL 525: Students will explore basic concepts in population and quantitative genetics, and focus on approaches to dissecting genetic variation in ecologically important traits across multiple scales. The topics covered in this course are broadly applicable to many areas of biology, ranging from microbes to plants and animals.
BIOL 526: A discussion-based course that uses on-line Collaborative Institutional Training Initiative training modules and supplemental readings to understand common ethical issues encountered in scientific research.
BIOL 528: This course provides graduate students an opportunity to refresh their scientific writing skills, focusing on clarity, accuracy, structure, ethics, and revision. Students will produce major thesis sections and practice peer feedback, aiming to refine their master's thesis writing through guided exercises.
BIOL 545: This literature-based course will cover the role of bacteria and fungi in symbioses ranging from mutualistic to pathogenic with eukaryotic hosts (including humans and their microbiomes). We will discuss the ecology, evolution, biochemistry, and cellular biology of symbiotic interactions. We will focus on the most current experimental approaches for investigating host-microbe interactions at the molecular and cellular level.
BIOL 547: This small lecture course explores our current understanding of the molecular and cellular mechanisms of cancer development, as well as current therapies used to treat cancer.
BIOL 551: An examination of the molecular basis of plant development and the applied uses of recent discoveries on crop improvement strategies. Emphasis on discussion of primary literature. Offered alternate years.
BIOL 575: This seminar course explores scientific research on the cellular and molecular mechanisms by which naturally occurring variation in genes results in medically, agriculturally, and evolutionarily important trait variation.
BIOL 576: This course will examine the general structural basis of membrane transport proteins; studying their mechanistic information, examining the actual body plans and structure of these proteins and evaluating the structure-function relationship that permits them to perform their task. The overall goal of this course is to acquire a unifying view of membrane transport mechanisms. Offered in alternate years.
BIOL 577: Introduction to the design and analysis of genomic research experiments. Genomics is the application of high-throughput molecular biology and bioinformatic techniques to questions in biology. Focus topics include genome assembly, differential gene expression, and genome-wide association studies. Primarily a computer lab course aimed at developing practical bioinformatics skills.
BIOL 580: An in-depth introduction to the analysis of sequence data at the gene level that combines concepts and theory in bioinformatics, molecular biology, and molecular evolution with applied skills development via computer-based exercises. Lab included.
BIOL 586: Molecular analysis of developmental processes controlling the formation of functional neural circuits. Emphasis placed on critical evaluation and discussion of primary literature.
BIOL 594: Laboratory investigations of cellular processes. Tissue culture methods and microscopy techniques, including immunofluorescence. Lectures will focus on optics and image processing.
BIOL 595: An examination of the molecular, cellular and genetic aspects of developmental biology in invertebrate and vertebrate model systems: fruit flies, nematodes, sea urchins, frogs and mammals.
BIOL 597: BIOL 202 & 325 or intro crse in zoology & ecology
BIOL 597A: An in-depth exploration of the current literature pertaining to biochemical pathways central to plant function, especially those involved in secondary metabolism. The focus is on transcriptional and post-transcriptional regulation of the metabolic networks and physiological and development functions of the end-products, but we will also examine the agricultural, health, industrial, and ethonobotanical, applications of phytochemicals and other plant products. Class discussions, literature research, and student presentations are key ingredients of the pedagogical approach used in this course. The instructor will present lectures and lead discussions during the first five weeks of the quarter. Students will summarize assigned papers and lead class discussions during the remainder of the term.
BIOL 597B: The class provides a practical introduction to how genetic methods can be used to address problems in ecology and evolution. As an applied course this class will stress general concepts and the use of quantitative tools in practical exercises while putting less emphasis on the theoretical details underlying these tools.
BIOL 597C: Investigation of recent and classic discoveries in plant developmental biology and some of the techniques and issues associated with the genetic modification of organisms (GMO).
BIOL 597O: The course will center on the primary literature in deep-sea research and will emphasize the history of deep-sea research, biogeographic and biodiversity patterns, life in the deep sea, the ecology of specific deep-sea habitats, and current issues in deep-sea conservation.
BIOL 690: Research contributing to a graduate degree program. Graded ''K'' until thesis completed. Repeatable up to 36 credits. S/U grading.
BNS 194: A course for College Quest students only. Emphasizes the relationship between brain structure/function and behavior through lecture and lab. S/U grading.
BNS 195: An introduction to the role of the nervous system in normal and abnormal behavior, thought, and emotion. S/U grading.
BNS 300: An individualized course of study not available through or replacing existing curriculum, to be arranged between one matriculating student and sponsoring faculty member. All academic policies and registration deadlines apply. Directed Independent Study courses cannot substitute for General University Requirements and are not eligible for tuition waiver.
BNS 301: An introduction to experimental design in neuroscience and coverage of the appropriate statistics analysis of neuroscience data.
BNS 302: Experimental design and writing in behavioral neuroscience.
BNS 305: This class provides a cellular and molecular understanding of central nervous system function. The physiology of neural cells will be stressed, from the ionic basis of membrane currents and synaptic physiology, to the unique challenges of neuronal cell biology. The genetic basis of normal and abnormal neurophysiology will be discussed.
BNS 306: Theoretical and emperical exploration of how different neural structures interact with one another to form functional circuits that transduce, analyze and integrate sensory information, assess that information with the context of current need and past experience, and then generate the neural activity that underlies learning and memory, attention, reward, decision-making, reasoning, executive functions, and emotions.
BNS 327: Introduction to laboratory methods and techniques used in cognitive neuroscience. Concentration will be on large scale brain imaging of cognition using EEG. Students will collect and analyze data from participants undergoing a broad range of cognitive paradigms.
BNS 328: Introduction to laboratory methods and techniques used in behavioral neuroscience. Two hours lecture and four hours lab each week; students will be introduced to basic techniques in histology, neurophysiology, neurochemistry, molecular biology, or behavioral analyses. May require live animal research. Repeatable to a maximum of 8 credits, including the original course.
BNS 330: Practical shadowing opportunities and direct engagement with healthcare providers in neuroscience-related medical fields across Bellingham. The internship involves weekly meetings with on-site clinical mentors, discussion of medical cases and relevant methodologies, and shadowing of clinical procedures. Repeatable to a maximum of 6 credits, including original course.
BNS 400: An individualized course of study not available through or replacing existing curriculum, to be arranged between one matriculating student and sponsoring faculty member. All academic policies and registration deadlines apply. Directed Independent Study courses cannot substitute for General University Requirements and are not eligible for tuition waiver.
BNS 401: A detailed examination of how behavior emerges from the function of the brain with a focus on neurophysiological mechanisms. Learning is based upon review and discussion of current literature in the field of behavioral neuroscience. The specific topic under investigation may vary depending on who teaches the class.
BNS 428: Laboratory based study of integrated neural systems underlying behavior, based on advanced techniques in histology, neurophysiology, neurochemistry, molecular biology, or behavioral analyses. Two hours lecture and four hours lab each week; may require live animal research. Repeatable to a maximum of 8 credits, including the original course.
BUS 200: This course introduces business as a social institution. Students examine key business functions and how they interact to create a well-functioning business while also considering the broader societal impact of businesses. Emphasizing critical thinking and contemporary perspectives, the course situates business within social systems, relationships, and collective goals.
BUS 310: Exploring career options related to individual student interests will take place in the context of both general career-related information and customized feedback. Professional workshops on topics such as professionalism, networking, interviewing, and etiquite provide a foundation for each student's pursuit of their own career aspirations and goals.
BUS 410: This class provides students with opportunities to document and reflect on all of their professional and career readiness activities completed as part of their CBE program. Students will engage in career planning and preparation as well as reflect on program-specific activities.
C/AM 200: A broad interdisciplinary survey course which introduces students to the study of the territory presently known as Canada. Topics include human-environment relationships; Indigenous peoples and settler colonialism; the development of present-day cultural, political, and economic systems; and the impact of US-Canada relations. An understanding of Canada is valuable not only to provide a better understanding of a nearby neighbor, but also to gain a better understanding of the U.S. itself.
C/AM 277: Canadian history from aboriginal occupation to the present. Also offered as HIST 277.
C/AM 300: An individualized course of study not available through or replacing existing curriculum, to be arranged between one matriculating student and sponsoring faculty member. All academic policies and registration deadlines apply. Directed Independent Study courses cannot substitute for General University Requirements and are not eligible for tuition waiver.
C/AM 305: Topics in Canadian-American Studies. Variable topics. Repeatable with different topics to a maximum of 10 credits, including original course, but only 5 credits can count towards major requirements.
C/AM 325: This course offers an introduction to Québec politics and Québec-U.S. Relations. Part I uses a historical-institutionalist approach to present the main conceptual and theoretical elements on Québec politics and offers an overview of recent evolution in Quebec’s political life. Part II discusses three crucial themes in contemporary Québec politics: the evolution of Québec’s identity; the future of Québec’s independence movement; and the road ahead for Québec’s international relations. Part III shows how Québec and the United States are integrated and offers an overview of the actors and issues in Québec-U.S. relations. Also offered as PLSC 325.
C/AM 331: This course explores the production of Canada as both a territory and a geographical idea. Topics include physical geographies, Indigenous geographies, geographies of settler colonialism, resource extraction, urban development, and de-colonial spaces. Also offered as ENVS 331.
C/AM 355: This course examines how news institutions, governments, and other media actors in the region — Indigenous nations, non-governmental organizations, and multinational corporations — produce their own media that renders cross-border regions such as Cascadia, the Great Lakes, and the Arctic as politically and culturally dynamic geographies. The course provides students with an understanding of cross-border media flows and their impact on the relationship between Canada and the United States. Students in this class will acquire an introduction to Canadian news media in the context of their relationship to U.S. counterparts — and vice-versa. Also offered as JOUR 355.
C/AM 365: This course introduces students to the history of Canada's economic development and contemporary issues in the Canadian economy. It will especially examine Canada's international economic relations, and interactions with its largest trading partner, the United States. Also offered as ECON 365.
C/AM 366: This course will examine in detail different features of Canada's business environment. Topics could include trade relations, energy and resource policy, immigration and the competition for talent. The emphasis is on Canada-U.S. comparisons and on features of the Canadian business environment that are of greatest relevance for the United States. Also offered as ECON 366.
C/AM 368: This course explores the tangled colonial histories of the U.S. and Canada, paying particular attention to Indigenous-settler relations. This course engages with Indigenous scholars in order to understand the Indigenous critique of the two settler states. In addition, we will interrogate the roots of colonialism and what it means for all people to work towards transforming the colonial relationships that are embedded within state structures. Also offered as FAIR 368.
C/AM 369: Settler Cities represent settler futures, settler ideals, and settler fantasies while attempting to erase Indigenous presence and Indigenous futures. Many North American cities were built upon Indigenous villages, actively removing Indigenous peoples to create settler spaces. As this class will demonstrate, the ongoing project of settler urbanization has not been successful, highlighting the resurgence of Indigenous communities across Turtle Island and the geopolitical extents of the North American settler-state. The course provides a cross-border assessment of Settler Cities between Canada and the United States demonstrating the pervasive systems of settler colonialism and the shared project of Indigenous Futures. Also offered as UEPP 369.
C/AM 375: Spatial Knowledge encompasses the production of knowledge through land-based practices. Through the course we will investigate the impacts of colonization on spatial practices and the current dominance of settler-colonialism on Indigenous communities and the continuity of Indigenous knowledge systems. We will explore both spatial knowledge across multiple scales of the Land from macro, meso and micro to the rural - urban divide. Also offered as UEPP 375.
C/AM 379: Examination and impacts of significant developments in the political, diplomatic, economic, social and cultural relations between Canada and the United States. Also offered as HIST 379.
C/AM 394: Examines key themes and developments in the history of the Salish Sea from the precolonial era to the present, with emphasis on the eighteenth through twentieth centuries. The geographic area covered includes both present-day Washington state and the province of British Columbia. Also offered as HIST 394.
C/AM 400: An individualized course of study not available through or replacing existing curriculum, to be arranged between one matriculating student and sponsoring faculty member. All academic policies and registration deadlines apply. Directed Independent Study courses cannot substitute for General University Requirements and are not eligible for tuition waiver.
C/AM 401: Directed research on a problem or in an area of interest. Required for all students enrolled in the major.
C/AM 402: Analysis and writing on the research findings in C/AM 401. A writing proficiency course. Required for all students enrolled in the major.
C/AM 405: Advanced Topics in Canadian-American Studies. Variable topics presented in seminar style. Involves theoretical discussions with a strong emphasis on student research. Repeatable with different topics to a maximum of 10 credits, including original course, but only 5 credits can count towards major requirements.
C/AM 406: Canadian political institutions and process, relations with U.S., current topics including regional tensions, the environment, and First Nations. Also offered as PLSC 406.
C/AM 410: Intensive survey course featuring expert instruction from WWU faculty and distinguished speakers from Canada and the U.S. Topics include: Canadian history, geography, government, culture, free trade and environmental issues, First Nations and Canada-U.S. relations. Participants are introduced to a variety of curriculum materials, visit Canada, experience its culture, and develop a curriculum project that meets national standards and expands their personal teaching portfolios. Repeatable to a maximum of 9 credits.
C/AM 430: Geographic investigation of cross-border resource management and other issues associated with the growing importance of the United States' cross-border regions, especially our northern border with Canada; selected trans-border environmental, resource management, sustainability, economic, and urban topics. Also offered as ENVS 430.
C/AM 441: This course explores geographies of resource extractivism in North America. It is based upon the idea that, at root, natural resources and attendant spaces are produced through political-economic and cultural systems; they are not pre-existing things. The course is designed to enable students to identify how these systems have shaped natural resource geographies at a variety of scales in both the United States and Canada. Also offered as ENVS 441.
C/AM 444: Work as research and/or management assistant with a local, state or federal government body, private organization, or university unit. No more than 10 credits in internship may be counted towards the major without permission of the chair. Repeatable up to 15 credits, including original course.
C/AM 450: This course studies selected works of Canadian literature important for their artistic, cultural, or historical content and contexts. Like Canada itself, its literature represents a "contact zone" between Indigenous peoples, French and British settlers, and immigrants all over the world. Students will engage in close readings of one work of contemporary Canadian fiction with additional material drawn from Canadian history, geography and culture, including films and media to provide context. The course outline will look different each session, with new themes, readings, and learning activities.
C/AM 489: A research seminar that examines how economic, environmental, social and political agendas affect the shared international ecosystem - Georgia Basin/Puget Sound. Course focuses on the interests of various stakeholders and the efforts taken to manage the cross-border environmental issues. The course involves cross-border travel and field work and thus participants require a passport. In come years, the course will involve collaborations with students and faculty from Canadian Universities. Also offered as PLSC 489.
C2C 201: Introduction to service-learning mentoring through a campus wide mentoring initiative designed to encourage under-represented, low-income, first generation, and diverse 5th -12th grade students to graduate from high school and consider post-secondary education.
C2C 202: Service learning through a campus wide mentoring initiative designed to encourage under-represented, low-income, first generation, and diverse 5th -12th grade students to graduate from high school and consider post-secondary education. C2C 203: Introduction to critical and cultural issues in education through service learning in local participating school districts. Required field work experiences are integrated into academic studies that connect multi-cultural civic engagement to structure their research, reflection and discussion. This integrated service learning approach promotes the development of new social perspectives and broadens students’ world views.

CHEM 101: A course for non-science students. Emphasizes the process of building scientific models for how matter behaves through the collection and interpretation of evidence. Applications to important societal issues will also be discussed. Lab included.
CHEM 161: Matter, measurement, dimensional analysis, stoichiometry, atomic and molecular structure, periodic trends, and molecular interactions. Lab included.

CHEM 333: Theory and practice of gravimetric, volumetric, potentiometric and spectrophotometric methods of analysis. Selected analytical topics such as ion exchange resins, non-aqueous solvents, chelates, extractions, chromatography.

CHEM 426: This course will cover basic macromolecule and polymer structure and processing techniques. Emphasis will be placed on modern synthetic methods for producing and characterizing these materials. The design, synthesis and use of polymers in specialty applications will also be discussed.

CHIN 280: An introduction to the principles used in the formation and history of Chinese characters and their relations to Chinese culture. The components of the characters are analyzed and compared with the new, simplified forms. Reading materials and class discussion provide practice in reading and writing characters. Calligraphy sessions provide opportunity to learn theories and principles of writing characters in 4 different styles (seal script, clerical script, cursive script and regular script).

All academic policies and registration deadlines apply. Directed Independent Study courses cannot substitute for General University Requirements and are not eligible for tuition waiver.
CHIN 301: Designed to help students achieve the third-year (intermediate-high) Chinese proficiency in listening, speaking, reading, and writing, It focuses on students’ Chinese skills in communication with expressions of abstract ideas, and in comprehension of multiple-paragraph texts of complicated grammatical structures and broader vocabulary. After a successful completion of the 300 sequence, students will be able to converse with native or near-native Chinese speakers on every-day topics in a variety of settings using tonally accurate, syntactically complex, and lexically appropriate language. Students will also be able to understand linguistic variety of regional/national usages within Chinese cultures. Taught in Chinese.
